<div class="lx-interactive lx-cards" data-learn="a05-adequacy" data-src="../assets/learn/data/town_year.json ../assets/learn/data/m03-capacity-expansion-2024.json ../assets/learn/data/cf_targets.json ../assets/learn/data/a05-adequacy.json ../assets/learn/data/path.json">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<p class="lx-eyebrow">The Plains Grid over 500 simulated years (seed 2025; illustrative fleet, resampled weather)</p>
<ol>
<li>4,000 MW of coal and gas units, 3,000 MW of wind and 1,200 MW of solar serve a 4,000 MW peak. Units fail at random.</li>
<li>Over 500 simulated years the loss-of-load expectation is 0.228 days a year (± 0.049 from sampling alone), above the 1-in-10 criterion of 0.1. In 410 years nothing went short.</li>
<li>Shortfalls bunch on summer evenings: 81% of the shortfall hours fall in June to September.</li>
<li>Each 500 MW added, demand response counted as supply, lifts a nameplate reserve margin from 105.0% to 117.5%, yet LOLE ends anywhere from 0.012 to 0.200.</li>
<li>Rated by the perfect MW that cut unserved energy as much, the five resources range from 89% (peakers) to 15% (solar) of their 500 MW (table below).</li>
<li>Three blocks of solar in a row: 15%, then 6%, then 3%. Beside a 500 MW battery, solar's first block rates 31%.</li>
</ol>
<div class="a5-tables">

<tr><td>Demand response</td><td>500 MW of load that can be cut, at most 4 hours a day</td><td>0.048</td><td>132 MW</td><td>26%</td></tr>
</tbody></table>

<p class="lx-hint">With JavaScript on, you roll simulated years, run 500 of them with a seed you can change, and rate each resource yourself.</p>

</div>
<div class="lx-datanote"><svg class="lx-ic" viewBox="0 0 24 24" fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.8" aria-hidden="true"><circle cx="12" cy="12" r="8.5"/><path d="M12 11v5M12 8v.2"/></svg><ul>
<li>A teaching simulation: the Plains Grid, its units, their outage rates and the resources added are illustrative, set so that the grid misses the criterion before anything is added.</li>
<li>Weather is resampled, not observed: each week of a simulated year is a real week of 2024 or 2025, shifted by up to a week. The extremes are days that happened then.</li>
<li>Real shapes: demand, wind and sun of the Southwest Power Pool (<a href="https://www.eia.gov/electricity/gridmonitor/">EIA-930</a>, 2024 and 2025); wind and solar scaled to EIA's 2025 monthly <span class="lx-term" data-term="capacity-factor">capacity factors</span>, as in <a href="m03-capacity-expansion.html">M3</a>.</li>
<li>Units fail independently of each other and of the weather. Planned maintenance, the network and imports are left out.</li>
<li>Simple operating rules, not optimized: the battery starts each year full, charges from any surplus and discharges only in a shortfall; demand response covers a day's first 4 shortfall hours. Better timing could rate both higher.</li>
<li>A simulated year is not a forecast; LOLE, LOLH and EUE are averages over the 500 years. LOLE is shown with its Monte Carlo error, which leaves out uncertainty in the weather history and the assumptions.</li>
</ul></div>
<p class="lx-hint" style="margin-top:10px">Need a refresher? <a href="03-balancing.html">Lesson 3</a> (reserves), <a href="06-three-jobs.html">lesson 6</a> (firm capacity) and toolbox <a href="k05-probability-statistics.html">K5</a> (Monte Carlo and standard error).</p>

::: {#explain .lx-sec}
::: {.lx-sec-h}
## What you just did, as diagrams
:::

```{=html}
<div id="a5-explain" class="lx-xgrid">
<div class="lx-fallback">
<dl class="lx-ideas">
<dt>Resource adequacy</dt><dd>Enough supply in nearly every hour, judged over many weather years and plant outages.</dd>
<dt>Loss-of-load expectation (LOLE)</dt><dd>Shortfall days a year, averaged over the simulated years; the common criterion is 0.1, one day in ten years.</dd>
<dt>Expected unserved energy (EUE)</dt><dd>Unserved MWh a year: how deep and long the shortfalls are, which LOLE does not say.</dd>
<dt>Reserve-margin screen</dt><dd>MW installed over the peak, demand response counted as supply: quick, but blind to when the MW show up.</dd>
<dt>Accreditation</dt><dd>The smallest perfect MW that would cut unserved energy as much, as a share of the MW added; it changes with the mix.</dd>
</dl>
</div>
</div>
```

```{=html}
<div class="lx-deepers">
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Analyst</span>Days or megawatt-hours: which reliability to match</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

- **Two measures, two answers.** LOLE counts days of any shortfall; EUE weighs each by its MWh. Demand response here removes many short, shallow days but less energy, so its rating depends on which is matched.
- **This lesson matches EUE.** In 500 years a count of days moves in steps of 0.002, too coarse to rate one block. PJM rates its classes by EUE too (Manual 20A, sections 2.4 and 2.6).
- **Marginal, not average.** Each block is rated against the mix already present. An average can hide how the contribution of the next block differs.

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
<details class="lx-deeper">
<summary><span class="k">Go deeper · Modeler</span>The simulation in five lines, and its symbols</summary>
<div class="lx-deeper-body">
```

- **Outages.** Each unit is up or out, in spells of random length: out for $r$ hours on average, up for $r(1-f)/f$, so out a share $f$ of the time.
- **Margin.** $M_t = \text{units}_t + 3{,}000\,w_t + 1{,}200\,s_t - 4{,}000\,d_t$ MW. A battery discharges only when $M_t < 0$ and charges from any surplus.
- **Accreditation.** The smallest $C$ with $\text{EUE}(\text{grid} + C) \le \text{EUE}(\text{grid} + \text{resource})$, by bisection: halve the range of MW again and again until the two match.
- **Unique, or a boundary.** EUE falls strictly while above zero, so $C$ is unique. If the resource leaves no shortfall in the sample, the smallest $C$ is a limit of 500 years, not zero risk.
- **Correlated outages.** Real studies tie outage rates to temperature (PJM's Manual 20A, section 2.3); open tools such as PRAS do this at scale. <a href="a09-hazards.html">A9</a> adds hazards.

| Symbol | Meaning | Unit |
|---|---|---|
| $f$ | forced outage rate: the share of time a unit is out | share |
| $r$ | average length of one outage, the repair time | hours |
| $t$ | hour of the simulated year | hour |
| $\text{units}_t$ | coal and gas units not out in hour $t$ | MW |
| $w_t$, $s_t$ | wind and solar output per MW installed | share |
| $d_t$ | demand over its own yearly peak | share |
| $C$ | perfect capacity: always available, never out | MW |

```{=html}
</div>
</details>
</div>
```

## Check yourself
:::

```{=html}
<div class="lx-myths" data-quiz="a5-myth">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="hours" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “An LOLE of 0.1 days a year means 2.4 hours without power each year.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. LOLE counts days with any shortfall, of any size or length. Here 0.228 days a year came with 0.70 shortfall hours a year, mostly short evening events.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="nameplate" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “500 MW of solar adds as much reliability as 500 MW of peakers.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. In this grid the peakers rate 89% of their 500 MW and solar 15%: shortfalls cluster in summer evenings, when solar output is falling.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="fixed" data-answer="myth">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “A resource's accreditation is a fixed property of its technology.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Myth. It depends on the grid and its mix: solar's third block rates 3% here, and its first block 31% beside a battery.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="margin" data-answer="fact">
<p class="lx-qtext">Myth or fact? “Two plans with the same reserve margin at nameplate can have very different LOLE.”</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="myth">Myth</li><li data-value="fact">Fact</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>Fact. Each 500 MW added gives 117.5% at nameplate, yet LOLE ends at 0.012 with peakers and 0.200 with solar.</p></details>
</div>
</div>

<div class="lx-quiz" data-quiz="a5">
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="count" data-answer="b">
<p class="lx-qtext">In 500 simulated years, 114 days had at least one hour of shortfall. What is the LOLE?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">114 days a year</li><li data-value="b">0.228 days a year</li><li data-value="c">0.1 days a year</li><li data-value="d">2.28 days a year</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>114 ÷ 500 = 0.228 shortfall days a year, above the 1-in-10 criterion of 0.1.</p></details>
</div>
<div class="lx-qq" data-id="share" data-answer="c">
<p class="lx-qtext">500 MW of wind cuts unserved energy as much as 79 MW of perfect capacity would. What is its accreditation?</p>
<ul class="lx-choices"><li data-value="a">79%</li><li data-value="b">34%</li><li data-value="c">16%</li><li data-value="d">100%</li></ul>
<details class="lx-answer"><summary>Answer</summary><p>79 ÷ 500 ≈ 16%. PJM's 34% for onshore wind is another grid's rating, from another model.</p></details>
</div>
</div>
<div id="a5-drill"></div>
```
